processing: Roasted after picking, as a pan-fired green tea; published detail on the steps that set the hooked shape could not be confirmed.
harvest_season: Spring, as is usual for Zhejiang green teas.
appearance_dry: Hook-curled strips of green, as the name gou qing suggests.
appearance_liquor: Typically a bright yellow-green, as with similar Zhejiang greens.
appearance_wet: Typically tender green shoots, as with similar Zhejiang greens.
taste_profile: Described as having a full aroma and a mellow taste.

brewing.notes: Typical handling for a pan-fired Zhejiang green: water off the boil, a roomy cup, and pour off before it turns bitter.

vintage_note: Like other Zhejiang greens it is bought as the current year's spring tea and drunk within the year. Earlier, more tender pickings cost more, and grades vary widely between sellers. Check the year on the pack and store it sealed and cool.
description:
Yang Yan Gou Qing is a curled green tea from Yangyan Mountain in Linhai, Taizhou. The name joins the mountain with gou qing, a word for the hooked green shape, and that shape is the first thing you notice.

The tea grows above 700 metres, in moist air and mist according to local government promotion. It is pan-fired after picking, though detailed steps are hard to confirm.

The cup is described as fully aromatic and mellow. As with similar pan-fired greens, it holds up to slightly hotter water than the most delicate bud teas, though over-steeping still turns it sharp.

Grades vary between sellers, so judge it by the leaf: tight, even hooks and a clean smell are what to look for.
history: It is named with Panhao among the teas of Linhai, and a Taizhou government page calls it one of the two most popular Yangyan teas, with a silver prize at the China International Tea Expo Fair as its stated award. Little is documented about when the style was first made or by whom.
